strengths: Novel application of LLMs to neural interpretability: Uses Large Language Models creatively to generate interpretable captions for voxel-level visual selectivity, addressing an important problem in computational neuroscience with an original approach.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Thorough evaluation at multiple levels (sentence and image), across multiple ROIs, with extensive ablation studies, cross-dataset validation on BOLD5000, and appropriate statistical testing.
Strong technical execution: Well-designed four-stage pipeline with clear rationale, appropriate model choices, careful hyperparameter selection, detailed reproducibility documentation in appendices.

Consistent improvements and rich interpretability insights: LaVCa demonstrates consistent improvements over BrainSCUBA baseline with detailed analysis of lexical/semantic diversity, inter-voxel/intra-voxel selectivity, and subject-shared semantic patterns revealed through compelling visualizations.
Cross-dataset generalization: Demonstration on BOLD5000 showing that semantic selectivity patterns generalize across datasets, supporting robustness of the approach.
Excellent presentation and clarity: Well-written paper with informative figures, clear methodology, logical flow, and comprehensive appendices that facilitate reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Individual components (encoding models, image search, captioning, keyword extraction) are all existing techniques; the contribution is primarily in their combination and application rather than fundamental methodological innovation.

Modest quantitative improvements: Improvements over baseline are ~3-5% relative (e.g., 0.237→0.246 accuracy), and image-level improvements are smaller and less consistent; while meaningful, improvements are not dramatic.

Limited validation of interpretability claims: Interpretability improvements are primarily quantitative (diversity metrics, prediction accuracy); lacks human expert evaluation by neuroscientists validating that captions are actually more interpretable or meaningfully capture voxel selectivity.

Heavy dependence on black-box pre-trained models: Relies on multiple external models (CLIP, gpt-4o, MiniCPM-V, Sentence-BERT) making it difficult to isolate which components drive improvements; potential for uncontrolled biases from these models.

Small sample size and generalizability concerns: Only 4 subjects in each dataset; no analysis of inter-individual variability; unclear whether captions and patterns generalize to new subjects or populations.

Insufficient analysis of failure modes: Examples shown are mostly successful cases; limited discussion of when the method fails, what happens with hard-to-interpret voxels, or percentage of voxels with uninformative captions.

Missing important comparisons: Limited baselines (primarily BrainSCUBA); no comparison with other recent neural interpretability methods, simpler keyword extraction approaches, or human-written descriptions.

LLM-specific concerns: gpt-4o used as black box for keyword extraction; limited discussion of potential hallucination, bias, or sensitivity to prompting strategy; no exploration of alternative LLM extraction methods.
Reproducibility issues: BrainSCUBA reimplemented by authors as original code was unavailable; potential for discrepancies in baseline comparison; method highly dependent on specific model versions.

Limited scope addressed only peripherally: Method focuses on visual cortex selectivity from static images; acknowledged limitations regarding multimodal voxels, individual differences, and generalization to other brain areas are not substantively addressed.

strengths: Well-executed comprehensive experimental program with multiple subjects, datasets, and thorough ablation studies examining component contributions
Thoughtful multi-level analysis including lexical/semantic diversity, ROI-level specialization patterns, and cross-dataset generalization
Good documentation with clear visualizations, implementation details in appendices, and appropriate statistical testing (permutation tests with multiple comparison corrections)
Addresses a timely and interesting problem of using LLMs to interpret neural representations in visual cortex
Consistent improvements over the BrainSCUBA baseline across multiple evaluation metrics and subject samples
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: the contribution is primarily in pipeline design combining existing techniques (ridge regression, image ranking, LLM caption generation) rather than novel algorithms or theoretical insights

Fundamental circular evaluation issue: captions are derived from optimal images used in prediction evaluation, making the validation inherently circular—high correlations may reflect this design rather than caption accuracy
No human evaluation of caption quality or accuracy—the critical question of whether captions truthfully describe voxel selectivity is never directly validated
Evaluation methodology relies on embedding-space correlations which do not demonstrate caption accuracy; different descriptions could have similar embeddings
Weak baseline comparisons: primarily against one recent method (BrainSCUBA) with no comparison to simpler approaches, human-written descriptions, or alternative neural interpretation methods
Encoding model dependency not adequately discussed—poor encoding models would select poor optimal images and lead to poor captions, yet this failure mode is not explored
Significant performance degradation on BOLD5000 dataset (~40% drop in correlation) suggests NSD-specific overfitting and questions generalization
Method design choices appear somewhat arbitrary: number of optimal images (50), keyword extraction strategy, and 'Sentence Composer' filtering lack strong justification
Limited scope: only 4 subjects, visual cortex only, fMRI data with limited resolution, and modest cross-subject reproducibility (Figure A11)

Unsubstantiated claims that captions reveal 'richer representational content' and fine-grained features in face-selective regions—these rest on statistical diversity metrics rather than functional validation

strengths: Novel and well-motivated application of LLMs to generate interpretable descriptions of brain voxel selectivity, addressing an important problem in neuroscience and AI interpretability

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation framework including evaluation at sentence and image levels, testing on two independent fMRI datasets (NSD and BOLD5000), extensive ablation studies, and proper statistical testing with multiple comparison corrections
Strong empirical results consistently outperforming the BrainSCUBA baseline across subjects and metrics, with clear improvements in both accuracy and semantic diversity
Rich semantic analysis beyond quantitative metrics, including ROI-level diversity analysis, word clouds, UMAP visualizations, and cluster analysis that provide meaningful scientific insights

Excellent presentation with high-quality visualizations effectively communicating findings, and strong commitment to reproducibility with detailed methods, hyperparameters, ethics statement, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the work primarily combines existing techniques (voxel-wise encoding models, MLLM inference, text extraction) rather than introducing fundamentally new methods

Insufficient justification of technical choices including why MimCPM-V was selected over alternatives, the specific iterative decoding weights (0.2, 0.2, 1.2), and why 50 optimal images was the initial choice
Incomplete baseline comparisons focusing primarily on BrainSCUBA; missing comparisons with classical semantic approaches and simpler baseline methods that would strengthen the claims

Limited analysis of failure cases: face-selective regions show notably lower accuracy without deep investigation into why, and no systematic analysis of which voxel types or concepts are harder to capture

Significant scalability and generalizability concerns: requires ~1.7 million external images for optimal image search, computationally expensive (−7s per voxel, −83h per subject), and only tested on visual cortex with 4 subjects limiting broader applicability
Small subject sample (4 subjects) and limited evaluation to only visual cortex; generalization to other brain regions remains unclear
Missing details on sensitivity to CLIP embedding choices, performance scaling with dataset size below full NSD, and true test-set generalization on novel images
